title: Static on the Line: The Noise in the Mind
reflection: When your head is loudest, name which kind of noise it is, then do one small thing that quiets the room instead of wrestling the thought. You are lowering the floor, not defeating the noise.

questions.q: In the radio picture of Conversation 3.4, what is the relation between noise and the signal you long for?
o: The signal fades whenever the mind is busy, and it only returns after a long spell of silence.
The signal is always broadcasting; noise is unwanted activity that masks it, not a failure to receive.
The signal is made by the mind, so a noisy mind is one that has failed to produce enough of it.
The signal and the noise are the same thing, and the only difference is the mood you are in.
questions.e: Under the music there is hiss, but the station has not stopped broadcasting. Likewise a quiet intuition, or the simple sense of presence, is always there; random thoughts, leftover moods and old reactions are static over the top. Clarity is the ratio of signal to noise.
questions.c: The signal is always there; noise masks it

questions.q: Dr Watson’s patient with depression says she cannot feel any small good things, such as a kind word or a sunny morning. What reading does the lesson give?
o: Those signals are real but sit below her noise floor, so the task is to lower the floor, not argue.
She has chosen to dismiss them, so the kindest course is to persuade her of what she is missing.
The good things are not really there for her, so she needs to look for bigger ones elsewhere.
Her taste for good things has gone for good, and no change of conditions will bring it back.
questions.e: Like a whisper across a roaring street, the quietest signals fall under the floor. It is not an attitude problem. You do not argue someone into feeling the good; you help lower the floor and it surfaces on its own. Dr Watson can say: you are not broken, the room is just very noisy right now.
questions.c: Small goods fall below a high noise floor

questions.q: “A calm mind is morally better than a noisy one, and its calm shows that its owner has done the right things.”
questions.e: Neither radio is a better radio. The calm mind is simply running in a quieter room, after rest, silence or a quiet week. Swamiji says this single idea dissolves a great deal of shame: noise is not a verdict on the person.
questions.c: Calm is a quieter room, not a moral rank

questions.q: Sarah describes busy chatter in her head and also a low background dread that never quite leaves. Which kinds of static are these?
o: Both are random chatter, since all the noise in a mind is of one kind and differs only in strength.
Chatter and a background mood: a hiss of scattered thoughts and a deeper, steadier noise of unease.
A stuck loop and a sudden spike: a repeating worry and a jolt that comes from out of nowhere.
Two sudden spikes, which come close together and are brought on by tiredness at the end of a day.
questions.e: The four kinds are random chatter, a persistent background mood, the stuck loop and the sudden spike. A lively mind that scans, compares, reacts and remembers throws off noise as an engine throws off heat. The trouble is only that, untrained, it runs nonstop and the floor stays high.
questions.c: Chatter and background mood are two kinds of static

questions.q: “Patañjali treated the companions of a scattered mind, such as pain, low spirits and ragged breathing, as obstacles to understand and ease, not as sins or weaknesses.”
questions.e: Dr Watson finds this moving: the picture closely matches what he was trained to recognise in anxiety and depression, and it tells a patient that this is an old, well-understood human condition and not a personal disgrace.

questions.q: Which three steady tilts does Swamiji say run beneath the random chatter?
o: Too much thinking, too much feeling and too much doing, which tire the mind over a long day.
A sense of not enough, a sense of separation, and a pull to repeat the old patterns.
Fear of the past, anger at the present and worry about the future, which colour what we see.
A weak body, a weak will and a weak memory, which are inherited and cannot well be changed.
questions.e: Not enough, separate, and stuck on repeat. They are like a camera with a slight blue tint: the bias is in the instrument, not in the scenes and not in the one holding the camera. So, like any miscalibration, they can be gently corrected.
questions.c: Not enough, separate, stuck on repeat

questions.q: Kai feels the old sense of ‘not enough’ and takes it as proof that he is broken. How does Swamiji turn this round?
o: He agrees it is proof, but says it can be fixed once Kai achieves enough in his work and life.
He tells Kai to ignore the feeling, since feelings of this kind carry no meaning of any sort.
The ache is the faint rumour of a fullness underneath; you feel lack only against a dim sense of it.
He says the feeling shows Kai is too proud, and that humility is what will make it go away.
questions.e: A thing that was simply small, and knew nothing else, would not ache about it. The pain of the tilt is the rumour of what the tilt is covering: fullness, unity and freedom pressing up through the noise. The very thing that feels like evidence of being broken points to something underneath that is not.
questions.c: The ache is a faint signal of the fullness beneath

questions.q: Kai wants less noise and says ‘just stop thinking’ has never worked. What approach does Swamiji give him?
o: Push harder against each thought, because a strong will is what finally brings the noise down.
Lower the floor: fewer inputs, a settled body, clean living, and one steady good thing to rest on.
Accept the noise as it is and do nothing about it, since any step only adds to the static.
Fill the mind with as many good thoughts as it will hold, so that no room remains for the rest.
questions.e: Fighting noise is like turning the volume up on static: you get louder static. You lower the floor. A steady thing such as the breath, a sacred word or a loved image stops the mind beating against scattered objects, and a finer thing lifts it too. Nothing is manufactured; the calm was always broadcasting.
questions.c: Do not fight the noise; lower the floor

questions.q: James tries a calm, unhurried first two minutes in class and fewer competing inputs. What is he testing?
o: Whether quieter surroundings make the class easier to control, which is a matter of discipline.
Whether the pupils have been taught enough, since a calm start gives time to check the lesson.
Whether attention that seemed absent was simply under a noisy floor, and comes back as it drops.
Whether a slower pace makes the pupils like him more, which would in turn make them work harder.
questions.e: James looks at his classroom as a noise floor. The experiment is to lower the room’s floor and see what attention was hiding beneath it. Attention that seems missing may only be masked.
questions.c: Test whether attention was hiding under the floor

questions.q: Dr Watson has a patient carrying shame about her state. What two things does Swamiji suggest he offers?
o: The reframe of a high noise floor, not a flaw, with one concrete step he would recommend anyway.
A firm reminder that her state is her own to put right, with a list of what she must change.
A promise that the noise will clear within a week, so that she can stop worrying at once.
A diagnosis of the exact kind of static she has, with no mention of what might be done about it.
questions.e: A true thing to tell someone who is suffering: not become someone else, but let us quiet the room and let what is already in you come through. Pair the reframe with sleep, less input or slow breathing. It carries no shame and real hope.
questions.c: Offer the reframe plus one floor-lowering step
